South Korean, U.S. and Japanese Foreign Ministers to Meet in U.S. on G20 Sidelines; Korean Peninsula Talks on Agenda?
The foreign ministers of South Korea, the United States and Japan will meet in Atlanta, Georgia, on October 30 (local time). About a month after their last meeting, they are expected to discuss issues concerning the Korean Peninsula, regional and global affairs, and ways to cooperate on energy and economic security.
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun (right), U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio (left), and Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu (center) walk together after meeting for a trilateral foreign ministers' meeting in New York on September 21 (local time). Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
View original image
According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Minister Cho Hyun is scheduled to hold a trilateral meeting with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) Foreign Ministers' Meeting that afternoon.
The three foreign ministers are meeting about a month after their September 21 meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. They also met in July on the sidelines of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) summit in Türkiye and the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) in the Philippines.
At this meeting, they are expected to discuss the situation on the Korean Peninsula, including North Korea's recent military provocations such as ballistic missile launches and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's visit to China, as well as ways for the three countries to coordinate.
North Korea is continuing its shows of force while touting advances in its weapons systems. On October 30, North Korea said through the Korean Central News Agency that it had staged a show of force the previous day involving suicide drones, cruise missiles and 600-mm multiple rocket launchers. The Joint Chiefs of Staff also detected around 10 missiles, including short-range ballistic missiles, launched the previous day from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea.
Whether the ministers will also discuss conditions for resuming U.S.-North Korea talks is drawing attention. The Lee Jaemyung administration has expressed its willingness to serve as a "pacesetter" for such talks, so the ministers may exchange views on ways to bring North Korea back to the negotiating table. At a parliamentary audit by the National Assembly's Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee on October 27, Cho said, "I think a U.S.-North Korea summit could serve as a catalyst for breaking the current impasse."
At their meeting last month, the three foreign ministers reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea and called on it to return to dialogue.
Minister Cho is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with major European countries on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting. A separate bilateral meeting between the South Korean and U.S. foreign ministers is also being arranged. Requests from various countries to meet with the United States, the G20 host, have been piling up, and, given Secretary Rubio's schedule, the possibility of a brief meeting remains open, according to reports.

TSMC Weighs Rare-Earth-Free Motors Amid China's Export Controls, Moves to Diversify Supply Chain [Taiwan Chip News]
TSMC Considers Replacing Rare-Earth Motors
Export Controls Threaten Semiconductor Component Supply Chains
Taiwanese Companies Pursue Alternative Technologies
Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s largest foundry, is considering adopting rare-earth-free motors to reduce supply chain risks arising from China’s export restrictions on rare earths. As even key components used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment become targets for supply chain diversification, Taiwanese companies are accelerating the development and commercialization of alternative technologies.
According to Taiwan’s Economic Daily News, Reuters and other sources on October 31, TSMC recently asked suppliers whether rare-earth-free motors could be used in its factory automation equipment. The move is intended to prepare for possible disruptions to component procurement caused by China’s export restrictions on rare earths. TSMC is including components that use rare earths in its equipment supply chain risk management and assessing whether they can be replaced.
In April 2025, China imposed export controls on items related to seven rare earths: samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium. In October of the same year, it announced measures to further expand the controls to cover additional rare earths, as well as related equipment and technologies. The scope of the controls extended beyond rare-earth materials to include technologies related to permanent magnet manufacturing, increasing uncertainty across global supply chains.
China postponed until November 10, 2026, the implementation of some measures announced in October to expand the controls. However, existing export controls remain in place, increasing the need for companies to diversify their supply chains. Since rare earths are key materials for high-performance permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, robots and industrial automation equipment, the semiconductor industry is also closely monitoring their potential impact on the procurement of manufacturing equipment components. The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that “defense and semiconductor supply chains could also be particularly affected if export licenses for components containing rare earth elements are delayed or denied.”
Adopting rare-earth-free motors requires more than simply replacing the magnets in existing motors. Their efficiency, torque, control performance and reliability must also meet the requirements of semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
In response, semiconductor component companies in Taiwan are drawing on their respective strengths in materials, motor design, and drive and control technologies to develop alternatives. As uncertainty over rare-earth supplies spills over into procurement challenges for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, companies are moving to secure related technologies and component supply chains ahead of time. China Steel is pursuing the development of alternative motors based on its materials technologies, including electrical steel sheets, while Fukuta is drawing on its motor design and manufacturing expertise. Shuo Yang is exploring ways to apply motor technologies that do not use rare-earth magnets, such as reluctance motors, in industrial equipment and cooling systems for AI data centers.
The Taiwanese government is also working to establish a domestic rare-earth supply chain. The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) currently operates a rare-earth pilot production line and, with government support, is moving forward with plans to build a separate demonstration production facility. The facility is targeted for completion by the end of 2028, with annual production of 500 tons of rare earths by the end of 2030. The Taiwanese government plans to use it to meet about 50% of the island’s domestic demand for rare earths.

articles.title: [Exclusive] “Chinese chips alone are a concern for AI” ... Scramble to secure high-performance South Korean DRAM - 매일경제
articles.summary: [Exclusive] “Chinese chips alone are a concern for AI” ... Scramble to secure high-performance South Korean DRAM  매일경제
articles.full_text:
They have already been receiving large volumes of DRAM and NAND flash from Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. But analysts say that as the volume of computing required by AI services in China grows and data center infrastructure expands at an unprecedented pace, the companies are finding it difficult to secure additional supplies through existing distribution channels and short-term contracts alone.
Because of the U.S. government’s export controls on advanced semiconductors to China, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix cannot export high-bandwidth memory (HBM), a key component in AI accelerators, to China. However, operating large-scale AI data centers also requires a reliable supply of general-purpose DRAM, which serves as main memory, in addition to HBM.
According to semiconductor industry sources on the 27th, as Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) rapidly ramps up DRAM production, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix still have an edge in the technology and mass-production stability of high-performance DDR and LPDDR needed for AI servers and other applications. “Unlike DRAM for PCs or smartphones, server DRAM—which operates 24 hours a day, especially DRAM for AI data centers—requires greater reliability,” an executive at a server company said. “When you assess actual performance, there is a wide gap between CXMT’s server DRAM and DRAM from Samsung and SK hynix.”
Analysts say Chinese CSPs still rate South Korean companies’ products highly for AI data centers, where stable operation is paramount. That is why they are also courting Samsung Electronics and SK hynix even as they build up a domestic memory supply chain, including CXMT, in line with the Chinese government’s policy of localizing memory semiconductors. The fact that Micron, a U.S. company, has effectively been pushed out of China’s domestic market is another reason Chinese firms are inevitably courting South Korean companies. After the Chinese government began imposing restrictions on Micron products in 2023, Micron announced in 2025 that it would withdraw from the Chinese market.
Daishin Securities projected that memory prices would continue to rise as server companies pay prices comparable to those for server memory to secure LPDDR supplies. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix need to maintain supplies to CSPs, which can be described as China’s version of Big Tech, if they are to secure market share in China. Along with the United States, China is one of the regions with the highest demand for AI data center construction worldwide.
According to a September report by semiconductor industry research firm SemiAnalysis, China has already built at least 24 gigawatts (GW) of AI data center capacity. That makes it the world’s second-largest in terms of AI data center capacity, behind the United States at 56 GW. An additional approximately 20 GW of data center capacity is under construction or in the planning stages.
Among China’s Big Tech companies, ByteDance is building out about 5.3 GW of capacity, while Alibaba is pursuing 3.9 GW, Tencent 2.4 GW, Baidu 1.1 GW and Huawei 1 GW. The country’s three telecom carriers—China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom—are also actively building AI data centers.
This reflects the rapid growth of China’s AI data center market. Chinese semiconductor companies are sure not to miss this opportunity. According to Omdia, Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC), China’s leading NAND flash maker, captured 38.5% of the mainland Chinese market in the second quarter, overtaking Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to take first place. It was the first time a Chinese company had topped the mainland’s memory semiconductor market.
As not only U.S. companies but also Chinese Big Tech firms seek to secure memory semiconductors, LTAs are becoming commonplace. The three memory makers announced in their earnings reports that they had signed LTAs with all their key customers. Supply contracts typically run for five years, with terms such as supply prices and advance payments varying from deal to deal. Industry sources say Apple is the only one among the Magnificent Seven—Apple, Microsoft (MS), Alphabet, Amazon, NVIDIA, Meta and Tesla—not to have signed a long-term contract. Industry observers expect Apple to sign an LTA within the year as well.
In its earnings announcement for the second quarter of this year, Samsung Electronics said it had signed LTAs with the world’s five largest data center operators. It plans to allocate at least 70% of its production capacity to LTA agreements. SK hynix has also said it signed LTAs with at least 10 parties. Kim Dong-won, head of research at KB Securities, said, “We estimate that Samsung Electronics has already secured about 80% of its planned memory production for 2027 through LTAs,” adding, “Hyperscalers are still competing to secure supplies of the remaining 20% of memory production not covered by contracts.”

articles.title: U.S., South Korea, partners back North Korea sanctions enforcement - upi
articles.summary: U.S., South Korea, partners back North Korea sanctions enforcement  upi
articles.full_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 29 (UPI) -- The United States, South Korea and other partners reaffirmed their commitment to North Korea's denuclearization and backed recent sanctions targeting Pyongyang's overseas workers, cyber activities and military cooperation with Russia.
A joint statement released Wednesday highlighted measures imposed this month by Washington, Australia and the European Union to disrupt revenue streams supporting Pyongyang's nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs.
"Their actions represent their efforts to disrupt the DPRK's ability to support its unlawful development of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missiles, and to counter unlawful DPRK-Russia military cooperation," the statement said.
The Democratic People's Republic of Korea is the official name of North Korea.
The statement was issued by the United States, South Korea, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Britain and the European Union.
The participants called for North Korea's "complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization" and urged all U.N. members, particularly permanent Security Council members, to fully implement sanctions resolutions.
Earlier Wednesday, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity accused of facilitating government-run information technology worker schemes that defraud American businesses and finance Pyongyang's weapons programs.
The department said North Korean operatives use stolen identities and fabricated credentials to secure jobs with legitimate companies, with the government taking most of their wages.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the operatives "weaponize sensitive data and extort businesses for substantial payments."
The targets included Russian financial intermediaries and a North Korean-controlled technology center in Russia that Treasury said had generated millions of dollars for Pyongyang.
The EU on Oct. 12 sanctioned three individuals and four entities over activities including North Korean worker deployments to Russia and an "arms-for-oil" trade. Australia imposed financial sanctions on two individuals and two entities, along with travel bans on the individuals, on Oct. 23.
The joint statement said the measures build on findings by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, whose reports have examined North Korea's military ties with Russia, IT worker fraud and overseas labor operations.
The 11-country group was established in 2024 after Russia vetoed renewal of the mandate of a U.N. expert panel monitoring sanctions enforcement.
Its latest report, released in September, estimated that North Korea's overseas labor program generated $450 million to $800 million in 2025, despite a U.N. deadline requiring workers' repatriation by the end of 2019.
An estimated 35,600 to 101,280 North Koreans work across at least 17 countries, the report said. Most are in China, while Russia has become a growing hub, including for workers manufacturing military drones.

articles.title: US, Japan, South Korea sign Arctic pact - Social News XYZ
articles.summary: US, Japan, South Korea sign Arctic pact  Social News XYZ
articles.full_text:
Atlanta, Oct 31 (SocialNews.XYZ) The United States, Japan and South Korea signed a memorandum to explore maritime and economic cooperation in the Pacific Arctic, as their foreign ministers discussed North Korea, regional security and threats to supply chains.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun signed the document on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta. Washington described their wider partnership as supporting security and prosperity in a free and open Indo-Pacific.
The US State Department said the memorandum for a Trilateral Arctic Pacific Partnership, or TAPP, was signed “to explore maritime cooperation and economic partnership in the Pacific Arctic”.
Its account of the meeting did not identify specific commercial projects, investment amounts or implementation deadlines for the Arctic initiative.
The ministers reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearisation of North Korea and full implementation of UN Security Council resolutions, according to the US readout.
That included restrictions on activities generating revenue for North Korea’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes. They also commended the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team’s work in exposing North Korean violations and evasion of those resolutions, the department said.
The ministers stressed the importance of peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait.
Rubio raised US concerns about China’s efforts to assert control over the South China Sea and what the department described as coercive behaviour in the East China Sea and Yellow Sea.
He also discussed Russia-China cooperation that Washington said undermined peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific.
Economic security formed another part of the discussions. The ministers reaffirmed their opposition to economic coercion and the use of supply chains as a means of pressure, the State Department said.
They reviewed implementation of a separate trilateral memorandum on deploying small modular nuclear reactors. The department said the cooperation was intended to draw on the three countries’ combined industrial strengths to advance global energy security.
The ministers also discussed areas of economic-security cooperation identified during a trilateral consultation in Seoul on October 15. They reaffirmed commitments in their September 21 joint statement and agreed to continue trilateral meetings at all levels.
Separately, foreign ministry officials from the three countries held a telephone meeting Friday following North Korea’s ballistic missile launch a day earlier, Japan’s Foreign Ministry said.
The participants included US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State David Wilezol, Japanese Foreign Ministry official Takashi Ariyoshi and South Korean Foreign Ministry official Baek Yong-jin. They said North Korean ballistic missile launches violated relevant Security Council resolutions, called on Pyongyang to stop such actions and reaffirmed close coordination.
The three ministers signed the nuclear-reactor memorandum in Ankara on July 7. Japan’s Foreign Ministry said that framework seeks to coordinate private-sector participation in reactor projects in third countries and strengthen Indo-Pacific energy security. Its objectives include identifying interested host countries, encouraging industry consortia and helping mobilise financing and investment, while maintaining nuclear safety, security and non-proliferation standards.
The ministers subsequently met in New York on September 21 during the UN General Assembly. Japan’s account of those talks described cooperation on supply-chain resilience, nuclear energy, cybersecurity and joint military exercises. They also agreed to advance international disaster relief and work against transnational organised crime in Southeast Asia, in collaboration with the UN Office on Drugs and Crime.

articles.title: Bank Of Japan Inflation Reaches 2% Target As BOJ Holds Rates At 1.25% - TronWeekly
articles.summary: Bank Of Japan Inflation Reaches 2% Target As BOJ Holds Rates At 1.25%  TronWeekly
articles.full_text:
The Bank of Japan inflation forecast is at a crucial crossroads, where the central bank says that underlying inflation is finally in line with the target of 2% set by the BOJ back in 2013.

This is due to the fact that wage increases, coupled with worker shortages in Japan, are pushing prices up. However, despite the current success, the Bank of Japan held its benchmark rate at 1.25% with an 8-1 vote in October 2026.
In addition, the central bank has kept its resolve about the possibility of additional hikes in interest rates depending on the development of the economy and inflation in accordance with its expectations. It shows that the policymakers are still concerned about keeping price rises steady.

Bank of Japan Inflation Forecast Remains Above Target
In its economic forecast for October 2026, the BOJ estimated that the core inflation rate will be higher than the targeted 2% for the next two fiscal years, after which it will move back to the target rate.
According to BOJ estimates, the core inflation rate will be 2.5% in FY2026 and 2.6% in FY2027, after which it will fall to 2.0% in FY2028.
The estimates show that the Bank of Japan inflation forecast will stay high in the near future. However, prices will stabilize as the economy recovers.
Labour shortages and increased wage growth are key factors behind this phenomenon. Japanese firms are finding themselves under pressure to raise their wages in order to be able to employ and retain workers. Increased wages could also help to boost spending among Japanese households.
BOJ believes that this connection between wages and prices will help to maintain underlying inflation near the target level of 2%.
Japan’s Economic Growth Expected to Improve
The BOJ anticipates that the economic growth of Japan will be modest in FY2026 but gradually improve after FY2027.
In accordance with the latest estimates by the BOJ, GDP growth will rise to 0.7% in FY2026 and to 0.7% in FY2027. In FY2028, the estimates for GDP growth rise to 0.8%.
The BOJ foresees that the economy will receive support from lower energy prices and increased household consumption.
Higher wages may also have an effect on consumer spending capabilities and motivate companies to invest. This could contribute to the recovery of the Japanese economy while backing the Bank of Japan Inflation forecast.
Nevertheless, the recovery process is under threat from international energy markets and imports.
Higher Energy Prices and Yen Weakness Add to Inflation Risks
BOJ highlighted some possible reasons behind persistently high levels of inflation pressures. These reasons were high crude oil prices, high prices of semiconductors, a weaker yen, and growing inflationary expectations.
The depreciation of the yen results in the increased cost of imported goods and energy resources in Japan. Being heavily dependent on foreign energy sources, Japan is vulnerable to increased oil prices abroad.
The increasing cost of semiconductors will also impact manufacturing firms, especially those working in the electronics and industrial segments.
These considerations are still relevant for the Bank of Japan inflation outlook since rising business costs will eventually increase consumer prices.
The Bank of Japan is also tracking inflation expectations. If businesses expect more price hikes in the future, they can increase their selling prices, while workers can ask for wage increments to cover their costs.
Markets Expect Another BOJ Rate Increase in December
The BOJ kept the benchmark interest rate steady at 1.25% in October, but its current policy framework indicates that there is room left for further increases in case the economy and inflation develop according to forecasts.
According to the Reuters poll conducted on October 20 and revised on October 23, about 70% of the surveyed economists predicted a rise in interest rates to 1.50% in December.
This would be another step towards the normalization of Japan’s monetary policy.
The Bank of Japan inflation forecast will continue to be a key consideration when deciding on future rate hikes. The Bank will keep an eye on wage bargaining, energy costs, consumer expenditures, and the yen, among other variables, before making a decision about further rate hikes.
The global financial markets will pay attention to any developments in Japanese interest rates as well.
Generally, the current Bank of Japan Inflation represents a significant achievement for the country’s economy. Although inflation is currently aligned with the 2% objective set by the central bank, the policymakers have to deal with the problem of ensuring price stability without putting any strain on the economy.

articles.title: Why Peace Remains Out Of Reach On The Korean Peninsula - The Friday Times
articles.summary: Why Peace Remains Out Of Reach On The Korean Peninsula  The Friday Times
articles.full_text:
According to Reuters news agency, there has been some speculation about a possible meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit scheduled to be held in Shenzhen, China, on November 18–19, 2026. The last meeting between President Trump and Chairman Kim took place in Hanoi, Vietnam, on February 27, 2019. During President Trump’s second term, North Korea has occupied a relatively low position on Washington’s policy agenda because of the war in Ukraine, the conflict in Gaza, and tensions involving Iran. Nevertheless, the United States continues to seek a breakthrough in its relations with Pyongyang to promote peace on the Korean Peninsula.
Following Japan’s defeat in the Second World War in 1945, the Korean Peninsula was divided along the 38th parallel, and North and South Korea subsequently established different political systems. After the three-year Korean War (1950–1953), the two Koreas embarked on a competition between their respective systems. South Korea concentrated on economic development, while North Korea placed greater emphasis on military buildup and nuclear development.
In the mid-1990s, North Korea, South Korea, and the United States pursued diplomatic efforts to manage tensions and address the North Korean nuclear issue. The United States and North Korea concluded the Agreed Framework in Geneva in 1994, accompanied by substantial measures to ease sanctions. However, disputes over the implementation of the Agreed Framework eventually led to its breakdown, and North Korea announced its withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) in 2003. Since then, Pyongyang has continued to advance its nuclear weapons capabilities while rejecting international demands for denuclearization. By emphasizing its status as a nuclear-armed state and continuing missile provocations, North Korea has ensured that the security threat on the Korean Peninsula remains unresolved.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), North Korea is estimated to possess approximately 60 nuclear warheads. Its nuclear ambitions have also extended to the development of intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) capable of striking the U.S. mainland. Although North Korea possesses nuclear weapons in practice, its position differs from that of India and Pakistan in that it remains subject to international sanctions aimed at achieving its denuclearization.
There are various impediments to peace on the Korean Peninsula. These include North Korea’s military buildup and nuclear weapons development; the persistent deadlock in inter-Korean relations and the question of unification; and the prolonged suspension of dialogue between Washington and Pyongyang following the summit between President Donald Trump and Chairman Kim Jong Un in February 2019. More recently, deepening military cooperation between North Korea and Russia and intensifying strategic competition between the United States and China have emerged as additional obstacles. As these sources of instability persist, the risks of armed confrontation and military miscalculation increase. It is therefore necessary to restore summit-level dialogue between the United States and North Korea in the interest of peace on the Korean Peninsula.
 Rather than prioritising military expansion and nuclear weapons development for regime survival, the North Korean leadership should devote greater efforts to economic development and the welfare of its people, whose living standards remain far below those of their South Korean counterparts.
One may ask why the United States remains interested in dialogue with Pyongyang despite the North Korean regime’s continued intransigence and threatening posture. Why do the United States and South Korea continue to explore diplomatic approaches when North Korea already possesses nuclear weapons and is pursuing the development of ICBMs? Why do Russia and China continue to support North Korea, and why has Pyongyang dispatched troops to Russia to participate in the war in Ukraine? These questions arise in the context of the North Korean nuclear issue and the heavily militarized boundary separating the two Koreas.
Unfortunately, sustained efforts at conflict management and confidence-building have not produced sufficient results to overcome the existing standoff on the Korean Peninsula. An expansion of trade, commerce, people-to-people exchanges, and tourism between the two Koreas could contribute to the normalization of relations and the resumption of a peace process. Unlike the collapse of the Berlin Wall and the unification of Germany, however, the prospect of a comparable outcome on the Korean Peninsula remains remote. Nearly eight decades of division and confrontation have made Northeast Asia a major potential flashpoint for international conflict. Against this background, the impediments to peace on the Korean Peninsula need to be examined from three perspectives.
First, the hardline and intransigent posture of the North Korean regime obstructs efforts to ease its confrontation with South Korea and the United States. Washington remains a key actor in the security of the Korean Peninsula, while Russia and China also exercise considerable influence over Pyongyang.
Nevertheless, if North Korea were to resume its long-suspended summit diplomacy with the United States, it could project to the world a narrative of engaging the American leader from the position of an already nuclear-armed state. Such a meeting could also serve to strengthen domestic cohesion and regime propaganda. It might further enable Pyongyang to reduce its dependence on China and Russia and enhance its strategic value in its dealings with major powers. Moreover, an improvement in inter-Korean relations could allow economically prosperous South Korea to become an important partner in improving the socioeconomic conditions of North Korea. Although the two Koreas share a common language and much of their cultural heritage, the legacy of the Korean War and continuing political and military tensions have made reconciliation difficult.
Second, there is a need for a strategic consultative framework to resume dialogue involving the United States, Russia, China, Japan, North Korea, and South Korea. Such dialogue should focus on confidence-building measures and verifiable, phased steps toward halting and ultimately dismantling North Korea’s nuclear weapons program. It should also consider ways to ease restrictions on the movement of people, capital, goods, and services, to the extent permitted by prevailing security conditions.
If the two Koreas, the United States, Russia, Japan, and China adopt a pragmatic and forward-looking approach, meaningful conflict transformation may become possible. This would require all six countries to demonstrate the political will and determination necessary to pursue concrete measures for peace. Russia and China could contribute by persuading North Korea to return to dialogue with the United States and South Korea. In this context, a renewed summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un could provide President Trump with an opportunity to reinforce his image as a peacemaker, while enabling both sides to discuss ways to improve their relations and promote stability on the Korean Peninsula.
Finally, rather than prioritizing military expansion and nuclear weapons development for regime survival, the North Korean leadership should devote greater efforts to economic development and the welfare of its people, whose living standards remain far below those of their South Korean counterparts. South Korea is an advanced economy that has achieved remarkable success through economic development. A fundamental shift in Pyongyang’s policy priorities could help remove some of the obstacles to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula.
It is hoped that, through pragmatic and forward-looking leadership, the two Koreas will gradually replace hostility with cooperation. The North Korean nuclear issue cannot be resolved in a single step. Instead, U.S.–North Korean talks should initiate a phased negotiating process and lay the groundwork for multilateral security cooperation. External stakeholders, including Russia, Japan, and China, also have a responsibility to support this objective. Such progress would ultimately help slow the pace of the regional arms race and ease pressures toward nuclear proliferation in Northeast Asia. Peace on the Korean Peninsula must become a shared vision of all concerned parties. Without meaningful progress, North Korea will remain economically isolated and continue to pose a major threat to regional security.

articles.title: Japan and Germany reaffirm support for Taiwan Strait peace - Taiwan News
articles.summary: Japan and Germany reaffirm support for Taiwan Strait peace  Taiwan News
articles.full_text:

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Tokyo on Wednesday and issued a joint statement. The leaders said European and Indo-Pacific security were closely linked.

Analysts say China has built strong technological competitiveness in semiconductor packaging as it concentrates investment in the field under U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductor equipment and materials. In advanced semiconductor packaging such as high-bandwidth memory (HBM), however, Korean companies including Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are seen as holding the lead. Heavy reliance on overseas suppliers for packaging materials is cited as a problem that must be solved.
Professor Yoon Chang-min, who previously worked at Samsung Electronics on semiconductor packaging technology and materials development and now teaches polymer engineering at Inha University, said at the Autumn Conference of the Korean Industrial and Engineering Chemistry held at BEXCO in Busan on the 29th, “China’s packaging technology is, in fact, extremely good,” explaining that “as exports to China of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment and other tools needed for semiconductor scaling have been restricted, China has significantly increased its investment in packaging.”
Semiconductor packaging is the process of protecting chips fabricated on wafers and connecting them to external circuits. Recently, as device scaling has reached technical limits, advanced packaging technologies that integrate multiple chips into a single module to boost semiconductor performance have become a core competitiveness factor for artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductors.
China is building up technological strength in general-purpose packaging and expanding its influence in the global market. Yoon pointed to the rise of China’s JCET as a major global packaging company, alongside ASE in Taiwan and Amkor Technology in the United States.
In advanced packaging, however, there is still a technology gap between Korea and China, according to this analysis. HBM, in particular, which vertically stacks multiple DRAM dies, requires extremely precise control over the properties of various materials inserted between the chips. Because each material expands differently when heated, products can warp or break.
“Semiconductor packaging is not just about making good electrical connections between chips,” Yoon stressed. “The most critical technology is integrating and unifying the materials that go between the chips.”
He continued, “Chinese companies have very strong capabilities in mainstream packaging, but they still lack sufficient experience in packaging highly advanced chips from Samsung Electronics or SK hynix,” adding, “In advanced packaging areas such as HBM, there are clearly still unexplored domains.”
Experts noted that Korea needs to strengthen its materials capabilities to maintain its competitiveness in advanced packaging. Yoon pointed out that Japanese companies hold an almost monopolistic share in core packaging material markets, and emphasized that Korean firms must not only develop materials but also secure evaluation infrastructure that allows them to verify performance in actual semiconductor manufacturing processes.
● Korean firms challenge Japan’s dominance in packaging materials
Dongjin Semichem, a Korean materials company that localized EUV photoresist (PR), a key material in front-end semiconductor processing, is now entering the advanced packaging materials market.
“Having developed PR for EUV, we are currently supplying it to customers,” said Dongjin Semichem Executive Director Kim Hyun-jin on the 29th. “We believe the technology gap with leading Japanese competitors has narrowed considerably, and that we have reached nearly the same level,” he said. The company is also preparing development of next-generation PR for high-NA (high numerical aperture) EUV lithography tools, which can realize finer circuits than conventional EUV.
In advanced packaging, however, Korean companies’ competitiveness is still considered weak. “Korean companies hold less than a 10% share of the global packaging market,” noted Dongjin Semichem Research Fellow Jeong Hak-ki. “It is the field we most urgently need to catch up in,” he emphasized.
Dongjin Semichem is focusing its development efforts on photosensitive insulating materials (PID) used for forming redistribution layers (RDL) and build-up films for packaging substrates. PID is an insulating material used in forming fine wiring that electrically connects semiconductor chips. Build-up films provide insulation between wiring layers in packaging substrates.
“One Japanese company controls more than 95% of the global market for build-up films,” Jeong said. “As the industry grows, we expect a persistent supply shortage,” he added. Dongjin Semichem is expanding its development portfolio to include underfill materials that protect the gap between semiconductor chips and substrates.
The company has not yet begun commercial supply of advanced packaging materials. “We are currently in a stage of close evaluation with customers,” Jeong explained. As technologies that stack semiconductors in multiple layers, such as HBM, continue to advance, existing Japanese suppliers will also need to develop materials with new performance characteristics, which Jeong believes opens up opportunities for latecomer firms.

articles.summary: "Changing Cell Structures to Overcome EUV Limitations": China’s CXMT Accelerates Memory Catch-Up, Bolstered by Massive IPO Proceeds, Domestic Demand and Technology Leaked from South Korea  https://economy.ac/

Authored On
Modified
China’s CXMT pursues higher DRAM density through 4F² cell structure development amid restrictions on EUV equipment
Massive IPO and demand from Chinese Big Tech strengthen funding base for technology development and mass production
Process information stolen from Samsung Electronics and SK hynix underpinned rapid growth
Chinese memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) is accelerating the development of next-generation memory cell structures. With restrictions limiting its access to extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment from the Netherlands’ ASML, the company is overcoming some technological limitations by changing cell designs themselves to increase density. Market observers expect CXMT’s development of proprietary technology to accelerate further. It recently raised substantial research and development (R&D) funding through an initial public offering (IPO) and is building a stable domestic demand base by expanding supply agreements with major Chinese technology companies.
CXMT Announces Plans to Launch 4F² RDIMMs
According to a report by technology news outlet Wccftech on the 10th (all dates hereafter are local time), CXMT President Cao Kangyu said at the fourth Integrated Circuits and Chiplets Conference held in Shanghai that day that the company would launch DDR5 RDIMM products using a 4F² memory cell architecture before the end of 2026. An RDIMM is a server memory module equipped with a register that relays command and address signals between the memory controller and DRAM chips to improve signal stability. The 4F² design reduces a cell’s footprint by changing the transistor’s current channel from a horizontal to a vertical orientation and placing a data-storage capacitor above it.
CXMT’s move is seen as an effort to overcome structural limitations facing China’s semiconductor industry. For decades, the DRAM industry has widely used a 6F² structure, in which transistors are arranged horizontally and each memory cell occupies an area equal to six times the square of the minimum feature size (F). Increasing density within this structure requires finer circuitry to reduce the area of individual cells. This is why major memory manufacturers, including Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and Micron, have aggressively adopted ASML’s EUV lithography equipment, which enables precise circuit patterns, as they compete to develop more advanced process nodes.
Why Was a 4F² Structure Needed?
Chinese companies, by contrast, face relatively significant constraints on scaling because U.S. export controls make it difficult to obtain ASML equipment. Finding alternative suppliers is also difficult, as ASML effectively holds a global monopoly on the production and supply of EUV lithography equipment. Against this backdrop, CXMT turned its attention to the 4F² structure. A 4F² structure can theoretically reduce the area of each cell by approximately 33% while retaining the same minimum feature size as the existing 6F² structure. Rather than using EUV equipment to draw more tightly packed circuits, it improves space utilization by changing the cell structure itself. It is considered a technological alternative that could allow CXMT to partially narrow the density gap with competitors that have EUV equipment while continuing to use its existing deep ultraviolet (DUV) equipment.
Since publishing its first research paper on a 4F² cell structure in 2021, CXMT has steadily continued developing related technologies and has recently been exploring the possibility of commercialization using existing DRAM manufacturing processes. Wccftech assessed that CXMT would likely begin by introducing some features of the 4F² structure based on its existing 15-nanometer-class G5 DRAM process. CXMT officially announced mass production using the G5 process in September. The process employs self-aligned quadruple patterning (SAQP), a technology that enables fine circuit patterns to be created using DUV lithography equipment.
IPO Strengthens Funding Base
Market observers expect CXMT’s technology development efforts to accelerate further. The substantial investment funds secured through its recent IPO support this outlook. According to Reuters, CXMT officially listed in July on the STAR Market, the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s board dedicated to technology companies. The offering price was CNY 8.66 per share (approximately USD 1.33), and the company issued approximately 6.68809 billion shares, raising CNY 57.92 billion (approximately USD 8.91 billion). This was the largest IPO ever by a mainland Chinese semiconductor company. Following the full exercise of the overallotment option, or greenshoe, the final number of shares issued rose to approximately 7.6913 billion, and total proceeds increased to CNY 66.607 billion (approximately USD 10.2 billion).
CXMT has said it will invest the funds raised in production process improvements and next-generation DRAM technology development. Specifically, a total of CNY 29.5 billion (approximately USD 4.54 billion) in IPO proceeds was allocated, including CNY 7.5 billion (approximately USD 1.15 billion) for technological upgrades to memory wafer mass-production lines, CNY 13 billion (approximately USD 2 billion) for advancing DRAM technology, and CNY 9 billion (approximately USD 1.38 billion) for R&D on next-generation DRAM technologies. In late September, the board also approved a plan to allocate CNY 13 billion of the excess proceeds to new technology R&D projects and CNY 5 billion (approximately USD 769 million) to the second phase of construction of a memory wafer back-end testing facility in Hefei.
Table 1. CXMT’s Progress in Securing Funding and Demand
| Category | Key Details | 
|---|---|
| Securing Investment Funding | Total IPO proceeds of CNY 66.607 billion, with funds allocated to production line improvements, DRAM technology advancement, next-generation technology R&D, and back-end facility construction | 
| Securing Customers | Signed a long-term supply agreement with Tencent and secured major Chinese technology companies, including Alibaba, ByteDance, Lenovo and Xiaomi, as customers | 
Strong Domestic Demand in China
CXMT is also stepping up efforts to secure stable demand by signing large supply agreements with major Chinese technology companies. In June, Reuters reported that CXMT had signed a long-term server DRAM supply agreement worth more than CNY 20 billion (approximately USD 3.08 billion) with Chinese internet company Tencent. According to multiple people familiar with the matter, the contract runs for three to five years, while supply volumes and specific product specifications were not disclosed. Reuters reported at the time that CXMT was also discussing similar supply partnerships with other major Chinese internet companies.
Indeed, CXMT’s customer base has already expanded across China’s leading Big Tech companies. The securities filing submitted during CXMT’s IPO named Alibaba Cloud, ByteDance, Tencent, Lenovo, Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo as major customers. As global memory manufacturers focused their resources on producing high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for artificial intelligence (AI) chips, supplies of conventional server DRAM tightened, prompting more Chinese companies to adopt domestically produced memory. This domestic demand base is expected to support CXMT’s capacity to invest in production facility expansion and next-generation process R&D.
Past Leaks of South Korean Process Information
Semiconductor process information previously leaked from South Korea is also highly likely to be serving as a springboard for CXMT. In January 2024, the Seoul Central District Prosecutors’ Office indicted and detained a former Samsung Electronics department head, identified by the surname Kim, on charges of stealing Samsung’s 18-nanometer DRAM process technology and using it to develop CXMT products. In May last year, prosecutors additionally indicted a former Samsung Electronics researcher, identified by the surname Jeon, on similar charges. According to prosecutors, Kim joined CXMT as head of development shortly after its establishment in 2016 with support from local Chinese governments. He led efforts to acquire related technologies by recruiting additional personnel from Samsung Electronics and South Korean semiconductor equipment companies. Jeon reportedly copied by hand and took out information covering hundreds of steps in Samsung Electronics’ DRAM process while moving to CXMT. Subsequent investigations also uncovered indications that SK hynix’s DRAM process technology had reached CXMT through a supplier employing former SK hynix personnel.
Prosecutors concluded that CXMT rapidly established its DRAM mass-production technology by using Samsung Electronics’ core process technology as its foundation and acquiring additional related technologies from other South Korean companies. They said CXMT’s developers modified and verified the leaked process information to suit production equipment in China and used it to become the first company in China to successfully mass-produce 10-nanometer-class DRAM in 2023. Courts have also repeatedly recognized that Samsung Electronics’ core technology was leaked to CXMT. Commenting on this, one market expert said, "Semiconductor suppliers’ data and know-how have astronomical value in their own right," explaining, "While some elements must of course be newly developed with each generation, a substantial portion builds on existing recipes." The expert added, "Acquiring a completed recipe can significantly reduce the time and cost of developing the next generation as well."

Executive Summary
Key Findings
- Japan is both a major user and an established producer of Sputter Equipment, supported by semiconductor, optical-coating, display, hard-coating and advanced-materials industries.
- Semiconductor production and R&D likely represent about 35-50% of demand value, with optical coatings, tool coatings and display applications adding exposure to separate investment cycles.
- Market demand could grow 4-7% annually to 2035; new fabrication investment and equipment upgrades support the outlook, while capex volatility and long qualification periods create uneven order timing.
Market Trends
- Advanced semiconductor and compound-material processes require tighter film uniformity, particle control and process repeatability, supporting higher-specification cluster tools.
- Research and pilot systems may range from roughly USD 100,000 to USD 1 million, while production platforms can extend from about USD 1 million into tens of millions depending on throughput and configuration.
- Domestic equipment makers compete alongside imported systems and subsystems, while service, process recipes and target-material compatibility influence customer retention.
Key Challenges
- Long customer qualification cycles and a 7-12-year planning horizon for major equipment replacement can delay orders and make annual demand lumpy.
- Vacuum components, power systems, process gas controls, targets and monitoring equipment create a multi-tier supply chain vulnerable to lead times and specialized parts constraints.
- Export-control screening, workplace safety, environmental rules and stringent customer quality requirements add compliance and documentation costs.
Market Overview
Japan Sputter Equipment is a capital-equipment market serving thin-film deposition across electronics and precision manufacturing. Sputtering transfers atoms from a target material onto a substrate in a controlled vacuum environment. System configurations include DC and RF magnetron tools, reactive sputtering, ion-beam systems and high-power impulse magnetron sputtering. The right platform depends on film composition, substrate size, uniformity, throughput and process integration. Buyers include semiconductor manufacturers, device and display producers, optical-coating firms, universities, national laboratories and industrial coating specialists.
Japan has a dual role: domestic manufacturers supply equipment and process expertise, while Japanese fabs and materials companies create a sophisticated local demand base. Semiconductor investment is an important growth engine, but sputtering also serves optical filters, data storage, solar technologies, decorative coatings and hard coatings for cutting tools. The market is sensitive to capex cycles and technology transitions. A system purchase involves not only the chamber, but also pumps, power supplies, gas delivery, cooling, automation, metrology, installation and process qualification.
Market Size and Growth
Market value is difficult to isolate because sputter modules can be integrated into broader vacuum-processing platforms and equipment shipments may include service, software and process packages. A reasonable structural forecast is 4-7% annual demand growth through 2035, with periods above that range when semiconductor and display investment accelerates. Orders are lumpy: one large fab or research program can shift annual demand materially, while a pause in construction can defer multiple tools. A single point estimate would obscure this capex exposure.
Demand could be 40-90% above the current base by 2035 if Japanese and foreign-linked semiconductor investment continues, advanced packaging and materials research expands, and existing coating lines upgrade. The lower case reflects mature segments, high tool prices and alternative deposition techniques; the upper case requires sustained investment and adoption of higher-performance sputter processes. Replacement and refurbishment provide a baseline, commonly planned over a 7-12-year equipment life, while process upgrades may bring forward selective chamber or power-system replacement. These are relative growth scenarios rather than absolute revenue or tool-count forecasts.
Demand by Segment and End Use
Semiconductor manufacturing and related R&D likely account for roughly 35-50% of Japanese demand value, including metal films, barriers, seed layers and specialized compound-material applications. Optical coatings and precision optics represent another significant use, while hard coatings for tools and industrial components support more standardized systems. Flat-panel displays, data storage, solar production and decorative coatings contribute demand that fluctuates with manufacturing economics and technology transitions. These indicative shares are broad because a single tool platform may serve more than one end market.
Production systems emphasize throughput, uptime, automation and reproducible film properties; research tools prioritize configuration flexibility and fast material changes. RF systems are useful for insulating targets, DC magnetron systems suit conductive materials, and reactive or HiPIMS processes serve selected applications requiring specialized film properties. Buyer qualification includes target compatibility, substrate handling, chamber cleanliness, recipe transfer and metrology. In Japan, customers often evaluate total process capability and equipment service over the life of the line, not simply deposition speed or initial equipment cost.
Prices and Cost Drivers
Indicative prices vary widely by system scale. Research and pilot sputter tools can range from about USD 100,000 to USD 1 million, depending on chamber size, target count, substrate handling, automation and metrology. Production systems can start around USD 1 million and extend into tens of millions for high-throughput, multi-chamber or highly integrated platforms. These broad bands are not quotations; options, installation, process development and service agreements materially affect delivered cost. Used or refurbished equipment may be less expensive but can require significant requalification.
Major cost drivers include vacuum chamber design, pumps, load locks, power supplies, gas controls, cooling, process monitoring and software. Target materials and consumables are separate recurring costs, and specialized targets can constrain process availability. Buyers also weigh yield impact, chamber uptime and service response, since a lower purchase price may be offset by downtime or rework. Currency movements affect imported subsystems, while supplier lead times can influence project schedules. Japanese buyers commonly compare lifecycle performance and process stability rather than use a simple price-per-tool metric.
Suppliers, Manufacturers and Competition
Japan has recognized domestic equipment suppliers serving vacuum deposition and sputtering, including ULVAC, Canon Anelva and Shibaura Mechatronics. These firms operate alongside international equipment vendors and specialist providers of vacuum hardware, power supplies, targets and process-control systems. Competition spans research tools, industrial coating lines and semiconductor production platforms, each with distinct requirements. Supplier differentiation rests on film performance, uptime, process transfer, cleanroom integration, application engineering and service coverage.
Customer qualification creates meaningful switching costs because recipes, chamber history and yield behavior are tied to a tool configuration. Buyers may therefore retain incumbent suppliers for established processes while qualifying alternatives for new applications or cost reduction. Domestic vendors benefit from proximity to Japanese customers and local engineering feedback, but imported systems can compete on specialized capability or global standardization. The ecosystem also includes target-material producers and vacuum component firms, whose collaboration can determine the performance of the complete process. No single supplier dominates every application class.
Domestic Production and Supply
Japan’s domestic production role is commercially significant: local equipment makers design and build sputtering platforms, chambers and related vacuum systems, supported by a sophisticated base in precision engineering, electronics and materials. Production is not wholly self-contained. Pumps, advanced controls, process monitoring, power electronics and specific targets may be sourced across domestic and international supplier networks. Manufacturing and final integration require precision fabrication, vacuum qualification, software and process validation; the resulting system is a coordinated equipment package rather than a single manufactured chamber.
Supply resilience depends on specialized parts, supplier qualification and access to field engineers. Some tools are configured for one process line and cannot be substituted quickly without revalidation. Large manufacturers maintain service and spare-part functions, while smaller research users may depend on distributor or specialist technician coverage. Long procurement schedules reflect engineering and acceptance testing as much as component fabrication. Domestic availability reduces exposure to some import delays, but imported modules and material inputs still leave the sector sensitive to global logistics and exchange rates.

A semiconductor boom and government spending pushed South Korea's third-quarter growth rate above 1%. The Bank of Korea said on the 27th that real gross domestic product rose 1.0% from the previous quarter, 0.7 percentage points above its August forecast. More than half of the surprise growth came from the semiconductor industry, which drove exports and capital investment. On top of that, fiscal spending delayed in the first half was concentrated in the third quarter, lifting the government sector's contribution to growth to 0.8 percentage points. Outside of chips, however, the private economy lost vigor. Private consumption fell 0.2%, the weakest in four and a half years, and the private sector's contribution to growth came to just 0.2 percentage points.
It is welcome news that the Korean economy is growing faster than expected. But the widening gap between growth figures driven by chips and fiscal spending and the reality of household life is troubling. Real gross domestic income, a gauge of purchasing power, posted its fastest increase in 49 years, yet consumption shrank — a sign that the warmth of growth is not spreading across the economy. Sentiment among small and midsize firms remains frozen, and as marginal companies and self-employed business owners are pushed to the edge, bank delinquency rates have climbed to their highest level in about a decade. If unexpectedly strong growth and the government's expansionary fiscal stance stoke inflation and lead to further rate increases, already strained low- and middle-income households will struggle more and the divide will deepen.
What the Korean economy has achieved this year is substantial. Even if growth stalls in the fourth quarter, the country can still post annual growth in the mid- to high-3% range. Led by semiconductors, where global demand has exploded, exports are all but certain to top $1 trillion for the first time. Per capita gross national income is virtually assured of reaching the $40,000 range for the first time in 12 years. But growth built on chips and expansionary fiscal policy is not sustainable. Economic imbalances from polarization and a policy stance dependent on fiscal spending weigh on future growth and gradually weaken the economy's underlying health. Fortunately, with semiconductors propping up the economy and buying time, Korea has an ideal opportunity to improve its fundamentals. Now is precisely the time to finely coordinate monetary and fiscal policy to address short-term conditions while moving quickly on bold structural reform, to resolve K-shaped polarization and lay the groundwork for sustainable growth.

Key Takeaways
- The semiconductor supply chain spans chip design, manufacturing, testing, packaging, and distribution.
- Disruptions and capacity constraints can cause chip shortages and raise prices across industries.
- Companies and governments are expanding production and suppliers to strengthen chip availability.12
What Are Semiconductors?
Semiconductors are critical components found in modern electronics. They are used in a wide range of products, from smartphones and laptops to automobiles and medical devices. These include microprocessors, memory modules, and integrated circuits found in these and other devices.
The semiconductor supply chain refers to the network of companies involved in design, manufacturing, testing, packaging, and distribution. The supply chain is complex, involving the coordination of a number of different stages, from sourcing parts and materials to the sale to the final end user.
One of the primary reasons for the pandemic-era shortage of semiconductors was snags in the supply chain caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, which disrupted production and shipping around the world. Lockdowns and other restrictions forced many workers to stay at home and semiconductor manufacturers to reduce their capacity or temporarily shut down production lines, while staffing shortages, quarantines, and port closures caused shipping delays that have slowed the distribution of chips. In its September 30, 2026 report, Micron identified AI-driven demand and insufficient memory production capacity as current pressures on memory chip supply.23
Why Semiconductors Matter to Today’s Economy
Semiconductors, also known as “semis,” or chips, are ubiquitous in modern technology and are used in a wide range of products such as computers, smartphones, cars, household appliances, gaming systems, and medical equipment. As a result, semiconductors are incredibly important for today’s economy because they drive innovation and productivity in many industries.
The technical definition of a semiconductor is a material (usually composed of silicon) that conducts electricity more than an insulator, such as glass, but less than a pure conductor, such as copper or aluminum. Their conductivity and other properties can be altered with the introduction of specific impurities, called doping, to meet the particular needs of the electronic component in which it resides.
The global semiconductor industry is a large and growing market, generating revenues of $574.1 billion in 2022.4 The industry is also a major employer, with hundreds of thousands of people working in the design, manufacturing, and distribution of semiconductors worldwide. Given their importance to the economy, semiconductors have become a key strategic industry sector for many countries, with governments and companies alike investing heavily in research and development to maintain competitiveness and innovate.
A Comprehensive Look at the Semiconductor Supply Chain
The semiconductor supply chain involves a complex network of companies, organizations, and individuals involved in the design, manufacturing, testing, packaging, and distribution of semiconductors. The semiconductor supply chain typically involves several stages, which will often include:
- Design and development: Some semiconductor companies, also referred to as “fabless” companies, design and develop new chips, either in-house or through collaborations with other companies. They are called fabless because they do not themselves fabricate the chips that they design and market.
- Fabrication: The actual manufacturing of the semiconductor chips is done by specialized factories called foundries. The foundries receive chip designs from the fabless companies, and they use custom equipment to create and etch chips onto a silicon wafer.
- Testing and assembly: After the chips are manufactured, they need to be tested to ensure that they are functioning properly. This is typically carried out by separate companies that specialize in testing and assembly. Once the chips have passed the requisite tests, they are assembled into products that can be used in electronics and other devices.
- Distribution: The packaged chips are then distributed to the companies that will either sell them to end users or incorporate them into their products, either directly or through distributors.
In addition to these main stages, the semiconductor supply chain may also include intellectual property (IP) licensing, disposal, and recycling.
All of these stages require logistics and supply chain management, which also includes inventory management, order fulfillment, and transportation logistics. Efficient logistics and supply chain management are critical to ensure that the chips are delivered to the end users on time and in good condition.
Challenges and Vulnerabilities in the Semiconductor Supply Chain
The semiconductor supply chain has become increasingly complex over the past several decades. This complexity has also made the supply chain vulnerable to disruptions, as issues or bottlenecks at one stage of the chain can have ripple effects through the entire system. These can include natural disasters; for example, in 2011, a major earthquake and tsunami in Japan disrupted the global supply chain for semiconductors, leading to shortages and sharp price increases.5
One of the most significant disruptions to the semiconductor supply chain in recent years was the COVID-19 pandemic that struck in early 2020, which caused widespread lockdowns and disruptions to global shipping and logistics. Lockdowns caused worker shortages, and companies at all stages were forced to reduce capacity or temporarily shut down. This led to shortages of chips in many industries. Car manufacturers were particularly hurt by these disruptions, which had the knock-on effect of creating a shortage of new cars, which drove up the prices of used cars to record levels.6
Another factor contributing to the vulnerability of the semiconductor supply chain is the concentration of manufacturing in a few key regions, particularly in Asia. This concentration has made the supply chain susceptible to geopolitical tensions and trade disputes, which can disrupt the flow of materials and components. For example, the United States has placed trade restrictions on Chinese semiconductor companies to impede China’s military modernization by limiting access to the West’s most advanced chips, which have extensive military and advanced artificial intelligence applications. On January 13, 2026, the Commerce Department revised its policy to allow case-by-case licensing of certain chips for export to China under security conditions.789
 In addition to these external factors, the semiconductor supply chain has also experienced shortages due to internal factors, such as manufacturing capacity constraints and changes in demand, as the industry is characterized by long lead times and high capital investments. When demand exceeds supply, it can take months or even years for semiconductor manufacturers to build new foundries and ramp up production to meet the increased demand.
Strategies to Mitigate Semiconductor Supply Chain Disruptions
To better deal with supply chain disruptions, several steps can be undertaken, but they are neither particularly easy to implement nor inexpensive. For instance, increasing production capacity and diversifying the available suppliers to reduce reliance on any one company or region requires careful planning and coordination—along with billions of dollars of investment. Likewise, companies could invest more heavily in research and development (R&D) to develop new technologies and processes to make chips quickly and more efficiently, but this would also take a great deal of time and money.
Because of this, governments can help defray some of those costs by offering incentives and tax breaks, and can help coordinate the establishment of new domestic production facilities. The Biden administration hosted semiconductor industry gatherings to spur collaboration and has created the Supply Chain Disruptions Task Force to mitigate semiconductor supply chain disruptions.10
These efforts seem to be working. Intel broke ground in 2021 on two new foundries in Chandler, Ariz.—a $20 billion investment—along with an advanced packaging facility in New Mexico.1112 Micron, another large chip maker, has also invested $15 billion to add memory chip fabrication facilities to its headquarters in Boise, Idaho.1314 GlobalFoundries, Samsung Foundry, Texas Instruments, and Taiwan Semiconductor are all building new fabs in the U.S. due to these efforts.
In addition to these efforts, consulting firm Deloitte warns that by the year 2030, more than one million additional skilled workers will be needed to meet demand in the semiconductor industry. To preempt a supply chain disruption caused by a talent shortfall, they advocate building new talent pools in new locations and leveraging educational and community partnerships as never before.15
What Is the Outlook for the Semiconductor Supply Chain?
Despite unprecedented supply chain disruptions in the semiconductor sector following the COVID-19 pandemic, the outlook for the industry is looking better. In response to the shortages, companies and governments alike have expanded capacity, sought more diverse suppliers, and streamlined operations. However, it will take some time before this additional capacity comes online and the full effect of these measures is felt by consumers.

articles.title: South Korea’s birthrate, the world’s lowest, rises again amid signs of easing demographic crisis - DD News
articles.summary: South Korea’s birthrate, the world’s lowest, rises again amid signs of easing demographic crisis  DD News
articles.full_text:
hSouth Korea’s birthrate rose for a second straight year in 2025, government data showed on Wednesday, in a further sign that a country facing a demographic crisis for nearly a decade may be starting to turn a corner.
South Korea’s total fertility rate, the average number of babies a woman is expected to have during her reproductive life, stood at 0.80 in 2025, up from 0.75 in 2024, according to preliminary data from the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
New births began rebounding in 2024 on a post-pandemic boost and government policies, after eight consecutive years of declines that saw South Korea register the world’s lowest birthrate at 0.72 in 2023, a period marked by sky-rocketing house prices and higher economic participation by women.
There were 5.0 new births per 1,000 people in 2025, up from 4.7 in 2024. That compared with 5.6 in China last year, 4.6 in Taiwan last year and 5.7 in Japan in 2024, where the trend remains downwards.
The pace of the rebound is faster than the government’s optimistic-case projection of 0.75 in 2025 and 0.80 in 2026, which forecasts the total fertility rate to break above 1.0 per woman in 2031.
Marriages, a leading indicator of new births with a lag of one to two years, rose 8.1% in 2025, after a record 14.8% jump in 2024.
“The biggest part is that marriages are increasing a lot, accumulatively,” Park Hyun-jung, a ministry official, told a briefing, noting a higher number of people in their 30s and shifts in social attitudes.
The sharpest rise in new births was in the capital, with Seoul’s fertility rate at 0.63, up 8.9% from 0.58 in 2024, though still the lowest across the country.
Shin Kyung-ah, a sociology professor at Hallym University, said the data needed more scrutiny because of statistical effects such as population composition changes.
“Still, it is meaningful as an indicator suggesting positive changes, which will, at least indirectly, also help make people become more positive about having a baby,” Shin said.
In a biennial government survey in 2024, 52.5% of South Koreans expressed positive views about marriage, up from 50.1% in 2022. The average number of children people ideally wanted to have stood at 1.89.
Last year, new births rose 6.8% to 254,457, the biggest percentage rise since 2007, while deaths rose 1.3% to 363,389, resulting in the population naturally shrinking for the sixth consecutive year.
ECONOMIC SHOCK
President Lee Jae Myung’s administration plans a five-year policy roadmap this year to respond to demographic changes, amid concern about an economic shock from an ageing population.
It also plans to expand policy support rolled out in recent years for childbirth, and to introduce measures to attract skilled foreign workers to offset a shrinking workforce.
“The government will further strengthen support for young people in their 20s and early 30s, low-income earners and the unemployed,” the Presidential Committee on Ageing Society and Population Policy said last month, citing evidence policy efforts were bearing fruit.
South Korea’s potential economic growth rate, estimated at around an annual rate of 2%, fell by six percentage points in the last three decades, more sharply than in most major economies, and is expected to drop to 0.6% by 2045-2049, according to the central bank.
Credit ratings agencies warn of growing strains on public finances from welfare expenditure. The country’s public pension fund, the world’s third-largest with $1 trillion in assets, is projected to run out by 2071.
President Lee has called for regional cooperation on demographic challenges and proposed at last year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit to hold the group’s first population policy forum in South Korea this year.
During visits to China and Japan in January, Lee also agreed with President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to seek collaboration on ageing populations.
South Korea’s population of 51.8 million is expected to shrink by almost a third to 36.2 million by 2072, according to the latest government projection in 2022.
(Reuters)

articles.title: North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report says - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report says  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
North Korean workers are being recruited into forced labour in Russia by a broker network using bogus student enrolments, according to a months-long investigation by an international law foundation.
The network brings North Koreans into Russia on student visas to skirt United Nations sanctions and labour law, as part of a state-sponsored work programme that helps fund Pyongyang’s ballistic missile development, according to the Global Rights Compliance report released on Thursday.
Operated by Russian businessman Vladimir Sokolov, labour-brokering platform KNDR.su markets North Korean workers to prospective Russian employers in agriculture, construction, industry and IT, charging a commission of 100,000-150,000 roubles ($1,240-$1,860) per placement, according to the Netherlands-based nonprofit.
In conversations with Global Rights Compliance investigators posing as prospective employers, Sokolov’s operations director, Ruslan Zhukov, said North Korean workers were enrolled in colleges they did not attend “to avoid the application of labour law”, the law foundation said.
Zhukov also described the workers being required to work 12 hours a day, six days a week, according to the report.
UN member states are prohibited from hosting North Korean workers under a 2017 UN Security Council resolution intended to deprive Pyongyang of funds for its nuclear weapons and missile programmes.
Despite UN sanctions, between 35,600 and 101,280 North Korean workers were based overseas in 2025, generating an estimated $450m-$800m for Pyongyang, according to an 11-country team that monitors sanctions enforcement.
Russia granted more than 36,000 visas to North Koreans in 2025, a fourfold increase from the previous year, almost all of which were officially for educational purposes.
Global Rights Compliance said the network also helped support Russia’s war effort in Ukraine, with Sokolov publicising at least two work sites with links to Moscow’s military-industrial complex.
Sokolov and Zhukov did not respond to requests for comment sent to Sokolov’s holding company, Black Horse, and KNDR.su.
Global Rights Compliance said Zhukov denied the report’s allegations, calling them “false, fabricated, and categorically rejected in their entirety”.
“The matter concerns exclusively students of a specialised college, sent to Russia within the framework of an intergovernmental agreement on the exchange of experience and the provision of venues for educational and industrial practical training,” a statement attributed to Zhukov said.
Lara Strangways, head of business and human rights at Global Rights Compliance, said the broker network pointed to deepening ties between North Korea and Russia.
“North Korean workers are being sent to Russian factories through a network that serves both states at once: Their labour props up Russian industry, including sites linked to the war in Ukraine, while the revenue they generate helps fund North Korea’s military programme,” Strangways said in a statement.
“What we are seeing is a clear exploitation of these workers as part of a cross-border system. If governments are serious about responding to this deepening alliance, they need to understand the role that forced labour is playing in sustaining it.”
North Korea and Russia have ramped up cooperation across various fields in recent years as Moscow became increasingly isolated on the international stage in the wake of its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Cold War-era allies ratified a landmark mutual defence treaty in 2024, with Pyongyang deploying thousands of North Korean soldiers to fight alongside Russian troops in the war on Ukraine.
