articles.title: Was North Korea behind the biggest crypto heist in history? - The Spectator
articles.summary: Was North Korea behind the biggest crypto heist in history?  The Spectator
articles.full_text:
When the world’s largest cryptocurrency heist takes place, it doesn’t take long for the finger to be pointed at one particular country.
North Korea is known as the hermit kingdom. It is ruled by a regime that isolates its people from the internet out of fear of outside information infiltrating its borders. But when it comes to cyberwarfare, not least cryptocurrency thefts, Pyongyang is anything but a hermit. With hackers stealing $6.3 billion overnight from the digital wallets of Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, it is no surprise that North Korea is the likely perpetrator. After all, the Kim regime will do everything and anything to get money, both for itself and its ever-expanding nuclear weapons programme.
Even though North Korea is yet to claim responsibility for the Binance hack, the theft is hardly out of line with Pyongyang’s past behaviour. Last year, North Korea amassed a record $2 billion through cryptocurrency raids. Not only was this a 50 per cent increase from the previous year, but more concerningly, the number of attacks were fewer. One such attack came in February 2025, after which the Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, would find itself short of $1.5 billion.
All these acts are committed by hackers forming the ominously-named Lazarus Group, which is organised, overseen, and led by the North Korean state (ironically, St Lazarus is the patron saint of the poor). Operating under the Reconnaissance General Bureau, North Korea’s intelligence agency responsible for clandestine operations, the Lazarus Group has unknown membership and uses multiple aliases when committing its thefts. The suspects behind this week’s hack go by the name TraderTraitor. In May 2024, TraderTraitor stole over $300 million from Japanese cryptocurrency exchange, DMM Bitcoin, by duping an employee of the firm’s cryptocurrency wallet system provider into downloading a Python script.
Under another alias, namely, ‘Guardians of Peace’, the Lazarus group infamously hacked into Sony Pictures in 2014, a month before the film, The Interview – which sees two journalists meet and eventually kill North Korean leader Kim Jong Un – was due to be released across US cinemas.
The $6.3 billion stolen from Binance amounts to nearly a quarter of the total size of North Korea’s economy. Weapons of mass destruction do not come cheap, however, not least a nuclear programme that is continually expanding in both quality and quantity. With $6.3 billion, North Korea could buy at least two short-range Scud ballistic missiles.
Illicit cyber acts and digital theft fund 40 to 50 per cent of North Korea’s nuclear and missile programmes and generate about half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. For a country still hit by sanctions – despite China and Russia’s ongoing help evading them – cryptocurrency thefts are a convenient way to replenish the Kim regime’s coffers.
In the early 2000s, North Korea earned foreign currency by operating state-run restaurants overseas, including in China, Russia, and Southeast Asia. Many, but not all, closed as sanctions and coronavirus struck. Fortunately for the Kim regime, the world of cryptocurrency and cyberwarfare is far more lucrative.
North Korea’s activities do not stop at cryptocurrency heists. It has gained notoriety for hacking into the computer systems of western commentors by impersonating South Korean academics (a scam which was once used against the author of this article). What’s more, Pyongyang has a vast global network of nearly 10,000 IT workers, a scheme which gained traction under the rule of the current leader, Kim Jong Un. Whether in China, Russia, or further afield, these workers have learnt how to master the art of employment fraud. After stealing identities of existing workers in Western companies, these operatives create fake profiles, apply for remote jobs in Western firms, gain access to a company’s systems – with the help of Western-based facilitators – and pocket the cash, sending nearly 90 per cent of their earnings back to the Kim regime. It is no surprise that North Korea’s annual revenue from these IT workers alone can reach over $500 million.
But is the Binance hack just the work of Pyongyang? Even though North Korea is the highly likely culprit for Binance’s latest troubles, we must not forget about North Korea’s new alliance with Russia. It is not just munitions, missiles, and manpower heading in the Kremlin’s direction. When Russia and North Korea signed a mutual defence treaty in June 2024, the two countries pledged to strengthen ties in and beyond the realm of security: one of the other areas was information technology. Cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang in cyberwarfare should therefore not be ruled out.
We must now wait and see as to whether the Lazarus Group, in all its guises, comes forward either to protest its innocence or accept responsibility for the Binance theft. The most likely option is silence.
Stealing $6.3 billion from the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange is no mean feat. It is a reminder to the West that we must take North Korea seriously. For as long as the country continues to develop its nuclear weapons, it will need to find money to pay for them.

articles.full_text:
A summit between North Korea and the United States is likely to be difficult within this year, a leading Japanese scholar has said, doubting that either side is ready for a meeting that leads to any "meaningful" negotiations.
Junya Nishino, a professor of political science at Tokyo's Keio University, made the remarks in a meeting with Korean reporters in Tokyo on Oct. 22, as U.S. President Donald Trump has expressed interest in meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un this year.
"I think a summit (between Trump and Kim) this year will be difficult," Nishino said, adding Trump's interest in resuming diplomacy with Kim stems more from personal rapport than from a U.S. policy aimed at negotiations.
Speculation has arisen that Trump may want to meet Kim on the occasion of his visit to China next month for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
"What we want is a meeting that leads to negotiations," he said. "I do not think either the U.S. or North Korea is prepared for that."
"A meeting could take place, but I doubt very much that it would amount to the kind of meaningful meeting we are hoping for," he added.
On South Korea-Japan relations, he said the two countries can keep their ties stable by managing historical issues rather than trying to settle them.
"Historical issues and unresolved questions concerning the past will remain challenges, but cooperation is still possible even when such issues remain unresolved," he said.
"The best approach for now is to keep expanding cooperation while managing historical issues, so they matter less to the overall relationship."
Nishino, a well-known expert on Korean politics and East Asian relations, credited the shuttle diplomacy between South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for the steady ties.
He warned, however, that the ties "require constant and careful management," as domestic politics shape each leader's stability and room to maneuver.
"It is important to manage the relationship carefully, so that domestic political instability does not spill over into diplomatic issues," he said.
"Japanese tend to judge South Korea by what its president does, just as South Koreans tend to see Japan through its prime minister. That is why leadership matters."
On the Sado mine memorial ceremony, one of the issues on which the two sides disagree, Nishino pointed to "a considerable gap" in how each country understands history.
"I don't think it will be easy to bridge that gap," he said. "Nevertheless, that does not mean a joint memorial ceremony is impossible. The diplomatic authorities on both sides will have to continue working to find common ground."
South Korea skipped Japan's Sept. 12 memorial ceremony for Korean victims of wartime forced labor at the mine complex for the third consecutive year.
Seoul's boycott came after the two countries failed to reach an agreement on key issues surrounding the commemoration, such as how to address the coercive nature of the mobilization of Korean workers.
Turning to South Korea's push to retake wartime operational control (OPCON) of its troops from Washington, he said it would bring major changes to the security framework on the Korean Peninsula and also have a "considerable" effect on Japan's own security.
He noted some may worry that a shift in the South Korea-U.S. combined defense structure could complicate the North Korean issue, especially Pyongyang's nuclear threat.
But Nishino said he did not think the worry was substantial, citing the United States' robust extended deterrence commitment to Japan and South Korea.
Japan is eager to advance not only trilateral cooperation with Seoul and Washington, but also bilateral security cooperation with South Korea, and has expressed its intention on several occasions, he added.
Beyond their bilateral disputes, Nishino said outside pressures are also weighing on both countries.
The Trump administration, which "views alliance differently from previous administrations," is having a "significant impact" on the two countries, he said. Still, he saw room to cooperate in areas, such as energy and supply chains, and to help steady an international order the Trump administration has shaken.
"I see this as a shared challenge for Japan and South Korea," he said.

articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics it reported an operating profit of 107.4 trillion won in the third quarter of 2026, equivalent to about $80.1 billion. This result was almost nine times higher than in the same period of the previous year, driven primarily by strong demand for memory chips intended for artificial intelligence (AI).
The growth reflects the advancement of technological infrastructure and the increased processing needs of data centers. Operators are expanding their capabilities to run AI applications, which is increasing the demand for memory and putting pressure on the supply capacity of semiconductor manufacturers.
Samsung multiplies its operating profit in the third quarter
Between July and September, Samsung it achieved an operating profit of 107.4 trillion won, compared to 12.2 trillion won in the third quarter of 2025. Revenue totaled 195 trillion won, although it fell short of market expectations, according to preliminary figures compiled by Bloomberg Line.
The rising cost of memory chips and sustained investment in AI infrastructure contributed to the South Korean company’s strong performance. Technology service providers and data center operators are increasing their purchases to meet the processing and storage needs of their systems.
Despite these results, investors remain attentive to market developments, the semiconductor industry is subject to cycles of expansion and contraction, so current growth does not guarantee that demand will maintain the same pace in the coming quarters.
Demand for AI chips puts pressure on semiconductor supply
The expansion of the data centers this is driving up demand for DRAM and advanced solutions for artificial intelligence servers. This increase in purchases is giving manufacturers more leeway to adjust prices and prioritize customer orders.
Samsung warned that chip supply shortages could worsen in 2027, this forecast suggests that semiconductor needs could continue to exceed available capacity, although market developments will depend on new production investments and the pace of AI infrastructure expansion.
Another crucial component is high-bandwidth memory (HBM), designed to quickly transfer large amounts of data and power the accelerators used in artificial intelligence applications. Its importance has increased as advanced computing systems demand higher performance.
In this scenario, the ability of manufacturers to expand production and respond to the needs of data centers will be crucial for the memory market in the coming years.
SK Hynix strengthens the outlook for the memory market
SK Hynix, for its part, presented solid results and favorable prospects on October 28, its forecasts helping to alleviate market concerns about a possible slowdown in profits associated with artificial intelligence chips.
The news also boosted investor interest in Samsung and SK Hynix, two of the main competitors in the memory market. Demand from data centers is transforming sales and pricing expectations, especially in segments related to advanced computing.
However, the sector’s evolution will continue to depend on the investment decisions of large technology companies. If spending on AI infrastructure if prices remain high, manufacturers could benefit from sustained demand. Conversely, a slowdown in investment would force a revision of sales forecasts and production plans.
Samsung announces dividends after record results
Along with its quarterly results, Samsung announced a dividend payout of 30 trillion won for the third quarter, which ended in September. The payout equates to 4,601 won per share, according to the company.
The decision comes at a time of strong growth for the memory business, which has benefited from the expansion of artificial intelligence and investments in data centers.
However, investors will also need to closely monitor the sustainability of these results, chip price trends, supply availability, and the pace of customer investment will be important factors in determining Samsung’s future performance.
With operating profit increasing almost ninefold year-on-year, the South Korean company is strengthening its image in a market driven by artificial intelligence.
The main challenge will be maintaining its responsiveness to growing demand, while the industry prepares for potential changes in the semiconductor cycle.
Looking ahead to 2027, memory price trends, chip availability, and the pace of data center investment will be key factors for Samsung and its competitors. The expectation of a tighter supply keeps the market focused on manufacturers’ ability to meet demand.

articles.title: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter - The Korea Times
articles.summary: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter  The Korea Times
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. economy grew at its fastest pace in a year in the third quarter, shrugging off higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East as consumers maintained robust spending and businesses doubled down on investment in AI.
The better-than-expected increase in gross domestic product last quarter reported by the Commerce Department on Thursday was in stark contrast to households' downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in President Donald Trump's record-low approval ratings and deterioration in consumer sentiment.
The advance GDP report was published less than a week before Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. Economists said the strong growth, together with other data on Thursday showing inflation accelerating and broadening out in September, bolstered the argument for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December.
The U.S. central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75 percent-4.00 percent range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."
"The consequences of an economy at full employment in addition to a historic capital expenditures expansion are on vivid display," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "If the Fed is looking for more information on why they should act to restore price stability they can find it inside a slate of robust spending ... stratospheric private non-residential investment and sizzling inflation data."
Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4 percent annualized rate last quarter, the quickest since the third quarter of 2025, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its first estimate of third-quarter GDP. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2 percent pace.
The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Fed officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2 percent.
Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8 percent rate in the July-September period, matching the second quarter's pace. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation. Households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending.
Business spending on equipment surged at a 20.9 percent rate, the fastest since the third quarter of 2020. That added 1.16 percentage points to GDP growth, the most in six years. Business spending on intellectual property products grew at an 8.4 percent rate, contributing just under half a percentage point to GDP growth.
Robust consumer and business spending were both sated with imports, which are a drag in the calculation of GDP. Imports increased at a 19.7 percent rate, the quickest since the first quarter of 2025, when businesses were front-loading orders to avoid higher costs from Trump's sweeping tariffs.
Imports a big drag
Imports last quarter sliced off 2.64 percentage points from GDP growth, which was more than offset by the strength in consumer and business spending as well as a 1.61 percentage point contribution from the rebuilding of inventories.
Government spending increased at a 5.3 percent rate amid a sharp rebound in federal government outlays, both defense and nondefense. Rising mortgage rates because of the Middle East conflict pushed residential investment back into contraction last quarter. Higher borrowing costs have overshadowed a moderation in house prices, weighing on demand for housing.
A measure of domestic demand, which excludes inventories, trade and government, accelerated at a 4.9 percent rate, the strongest since the second quarter of 2021. Final sales to private domestic purchasers grew at a 4.6 percent rate in the second quarter.
While inflation subsided after surging in the April-June quarter, price pressures picked up at the end of the third quarter. The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index increased 0.5 percent in September after rising 0.3 percent in August, the BEA said in a separate report.
In the 12 months through September, PCE inflation advanced 3.6 percent after an unrevised 3.4 percent rise in August. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the PCE Price Index rose 0.3 percent over the month after gaining 0.3 percent in August.
The so-called core PCE inflation increased 3.1 percent year-on-year in September after advancing 3.0 percent in August. The Fed tracks the PCE price measures for its 2 percent inflation target. Rising inflation, with average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon as the US-Israeli war with Iran drags on, left economists anticipating a slowdown in economic growth by year end.
Income at the disposal of households after accounting for inflation dropped 0.3 percent last month. Inflation-adjusted consumer spending was unchanged in September, putting consumption on a weaker growth path heading into the fourth quarter.
Economists also expected some moderation on AI-related spending as investors are focusing on the rising costs of long-term projects in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did not expect this pillar of support to weaken.

articles.title: Washington’s Overlooked Leverage Over China’s Chip Ambitions - Lawfare
articles.summary: Washington’s Overlooked Leverage Over China’s Chip Ambitions  Lawfare
articles.full_text:
Later this year, China’s leading chipmakers may receive a domestically built advanced lithography machine, which prints tiny circuit patterns onto silicon. Its arrival marks a step toward a Chinese alternative to ASML (originally Advanced Semiconductor Materials Lithography), the Dutch company that dominates this equipment market. China relies on just 343 deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines for advanced chipmaking because existing export controls prevent it from acquiring ASML’s more advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) machines or even new DUV ones. These DUV tools can substitute for EUV in some advanced processes but require more manufacturing steps, costs, and production time.
But building a machine does not make it production-ready. China still has to transition from “it works” to “it works every day.” That requires repeatedly, accurately, and quickly printing aligned nanometer (nm)-scale circuit patterns. Continued Western equipment servicing in Chinese fabs—or chip factories—could help China cross the gap. The next few months could be especially consequential as China tries to qualify its domestic scanners for mass production. These benefits of mass producing Chinese DUV scanners are not just hypothetical. Washington’s new tool sale restrictions might slow China’s artificial intelligence (AI) and military chipmaking, but China still makes advanced chips with regularly serviced ASML DUV machines.
Congress has proposed broader servicing restrictions, but the Netherlands has opposed extending U.S. controls over ASML. Washington already has a narrower option, though. It can enforce existing rules against servicing specific export-regulated items connected to export control violations, slowing China’s effort to make its own scanners production-ready
China’s Hardest Work Is Post-prototype
Fabs build circuits on silicon discs called wafers. Lithography machines, also called scanners, use light to print patterns onto those wafers. China’s new machine uses immersion DUV lithography, which adds water between the lens and wafer to print finer patterns. Immersion DUV uses 193 nm light compared to EUV’s much shorter 13.5 nm wavelength. Shorter wavelengths print smaller features in fewer steps, making advanced chipmaking cheaper and faster. Fab engineers can compensate for DUV’s longer wavelength by repeating multi-patterning steps on a single circuit layer. SMIC already uses DUV to make 7 nm and smaller chips. Since existing DUV scanners let SMIC continue making advanced chips despite U.S. export controls, limiting China’s homegrown DUV capabilities is critical. Still, compared to EUV, each additional DUV patterning step increases production time, costs, and defects.
EUV access remains a major U.S. and allied chipmaking advantage. But potential homegrown DUV machines still matter. If Chinese engineers make those scanners reliable enough for mass production, China’s fabs could significantly expand advanced domestic chip production. Because advanced fabs use both DUV and EUV for different chip layers, DUV would remain incredibly useful even if China eventually develops viable EUV machines.
On July 27, The Information reported that a state-backed Shanghai company had begun producing China’s first domestic immersion DUV machines. Reuters subsequently identified the firm as Shanghai Aishengna Electronic Technology Group, citing an anonymous person familiar with the matter. Founded just three years ago, the secretive firm lacks even a website but has roughly $1 billion in registered capital and two state-owned shareholders. After absorbing teams from Huawei-linked Yuliangsheng, which began testing a DUV prototype in 2025, and Shanghai Micro Electronics Equipment (SMEE), Aishengna now plans to produce five systems this year and 20 in 2027. These could help China go from producing no more than 20,000 7-nm chips per month in early 2026 to 100,000 by 2028. Its prospective 2026 customers include major Chinese chipmakers SMIC, Hua Hong Semiconductor, and CXMT.
While these production targets are eye-catching, they do not yet translate into successful chip manufacturing. ASML shipped 131 immersion DUV systems in 2025 and still captures over 99 percent of the market. Besides matching a mature ASML scanner’s ability to print fine patterns, Aishengna must align successive circuit layers on each wafer precisely and reliably. Chinese fabs still need months or longer to test homegrown DUV machines’ accuracy, reliability, and compatibility with other equipment before integrating them into mass production. Even if China’s “homegrown” DUV machines can effectively substitute for ASML’s, Aishengna’s dependence on key Japanese scanner components and local supplier delays constrain machine output.
China has historically sought overseas expertise for its chipmaking efforts. Reuters reported in December 2025 that former ASML engineers had helped build a separate EUV light-generating prototype in Shenzhen. China’s DUV efforts may be similarly accelerated. Permitting foreign technicians to continue China-based servicing and training efforts thus accelerates China’s homegrown chipmaking push. After all, how quickly China closes the remaining gap depends heavily on how much its engineers can learn.
Service Calls Teach Valuable Lessons
Working fabs equipped with advanced foreign tools simplify qualifying a homegrown machine for mass production. Chinese engineers can benchmark a prototype Aishengna scanner against a well-serviced ASML fleet. They could adapt ASML’s processes to maximize Aishengna output and compatibility with other chipmaking tools.
“Servicing” might sound like a technician changing a part and leaving, but for semiconductor manufacturing, it is much closer to sustained co-production. Western equipment vendors maintain software, replace components, diagnose performance, increase the share of usable chips (yield), and train local fab engineers. ASML explicitly describes “on-site knowledge transfer sessions” as part of its customer support.
ASML’s Chinese operations reveal an extensive support footprint. The company writes software to improve lithography in Shenzhen, builds chip measurement and inspection modules in Beijing, and trains customer engineers to troubleshoot and maintain DUV systems in Shanghai. China accounted for almost a third of ASML’s $37.8 billion in total 2025 revenue.
Although ASML’s support is directed at customers, better-supported Chinese fabs are optimal testing grounds for domestic replacements. Teaching fab engineers to fix alignment errors and improve yield on ASML tools helps them apply proven techniques to homegrown DUV equipment. Allied and U.S. servicing, including by Dutch firm ASML, can thus help local fabs make export-controlled 7 nm Huawei Ascend chips today while teaching China how to replace those tools tomorrow.
Current Controls Leave Servicing Gaps
Existing export restrictions block specific advanced chipmaking equipment, software, and technology shipments to China, and restrict certain U.S. citizens and companies from supporting Chinese chip development. But Dutch and Japanese vendors, along with nonrestricted Americans, can still service many Chinese DUV machines.
Congress has proposed a broad response. The MATCH Act would restrict equipment servicing at covered Chinese facilities, including those operated by SMIC, Hua Hong, CXMT, YMTC, Huawei, and Aishengna. It would also seek equivalent controls from allies such as the Netherlands and Japan, with U.S. restrictions extending to covered foreign-made equipment otherwise. The bill helps address the right problem but is moving too slowly.
The MATCH Act cleared the House Foreign Affairs Committee on April 22, and its sponsors seek to include it in the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027. A July 14 Senate procedural vote failed to advance the defense bill to debate but did not reject MATCH itself. Senate Democrats were still pushing for floor action on MATCH and two other chip-related bills (the Chip Security Act and AI OVERWATCH Act) as of Oct. 13. Even if the bill passes, however, the introduced Senate text allows further delays of 150 days or longer. The Dutch and Japanese governments have opposed the measure’s extraterritorial reach.
Aishengna’s first deliveries are expected this year. The next few months therefore pose a critical window: Restricting servicing during Aishengna scanner qualification would make transitioning to mass production significantly harder. While continued DUV restrictions after Aishengna qualifies its machines may still somewhat disrupt Chinese chip production, they would be much less effective as Chinese toolmakers will have already learned what they need from allied and U.S. service providers.
Commerce Already Has a Lever
The Department of Commerce does not need new legislation to enforce General Prohibition 10 (GP10), which blocks export control-violating items from being bought, financed, transported, or serviced. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which administers U.S. export controls, already prohibits servicing items subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) when the provider knows that a violation has occurred, is about to occur, or is intended to occur in connection with the item. The knowledge standard includes awareness of a high probability, which can be inferred from conscious disregard or willful avoidance of facts.
While later unauthorized transfers or license breaches can trigger GP10, servicing lawfully exported equipment pre-controls is not automatically banned. For foreign-made equipment, U.S.-content and foreign-direct-product rules determine jurisdiction. BIS may maintain jurisdiction over a component but not the whole scanner.
GP10 is a scalpel. But semiconductor tools are complex, and a scalpel can still cut deeply. Blocking service to an indispensable component or software can impair an entire production line. The commercial effects could extend further

EU preference for domestic production raises localization burdens for foreign automakers
Chinese manufacturers, already facing tariffs, expand production partnerships with European companies
Europe’s drive to reduce dependence on China also hinges on securing alternative supply chains
The European Union (EU) is moving to protect its automotive industry by proposing domestic production and component-sourcing requirements for electric vehicle purchase incentives and public procurement. With a proposal requiring EU-made components to account for at least 70% of total component value, excluding batteries, foreign automakers operating in Europe face a growing need to reassess their local manufacturing and sourcing strategies. Chinese manufacturers, in particular, have relied on Europe to generate profits but now face constraints on relocating production as local investment conditions compound existing tariff burdens. Yet the EU itself lacks sufficient alternative supply chains for Chinese battery materials, leaving it with the challenge of building its domestic manufacturing base in step with tighter localization requirements.
EV Incentives to Require 70% EU-Made Content
According to European news outlet Euronews on October 6 (all dates hereafter refer to local time), the EU is pursuing domestic production and sourcing requirements for electric vehicle purchase incentives. The European Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) would make vehicles eligible for support only if they contain a specified share of EU-made components. The covered categories are battery electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles. The proposal would attach these conditions to support schemes administered by national and local governments and apply origin requirements to public procurement involving vehicle purchases or leases. To qualify, vehicles must first be assembled within the EU. EU-made components must also account for at least 70% of total vehicle component value, excluding the battery. That share would be calculated using the ex-works price of each component. The Commission’s proposal would apply these baseline requirements to public support schemes introduced or renewed from six months after the legislation enters into force.
Batteries, which are excluded from the vehicle component calculation, would be subject to separate localization requirements. Initially, at least three main battery components, including the cells, would have to be EU-made. Three years after the legislation enters into force, that minimum would rise to five. At that stage, cathode active materials and battery management systems (BMS), alongside battery cells, would become mandatory EU-made components. Additional sourcing requirements would also apply to electric drivetrains and main electronic systems from the three-year mark. Each category would need to achieve an EU-made share of at least 50%, calculated using component ex-works prices. The proposal includes a derogation allowing small electric vehicles classified as M1E to meet selected requirements. Provided they are assembled within the EU, these vehicles could qualify by satisfying either of two conditions: an EU-made share of 70% for vehicle components excluding the battery, or the use of at least three EU-made main battery components, including the cells.
Table 1. Draft Localization Requirements for EU EV Purchase Incentives and Public Procurement
| Category | Key Provisions | 
|---|---|
| Scope | Public purchase incentives and public-sector purchases or leases of battery electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles | 
| Baseline requirements | Vehicle assembly within the EU and an EU-made share of at least 70% of total component value, excluding the battery Share calculated using component ex-works prices | 
| Baseline implementation | Applies to public support schemes introduced or renewed from six months after the legislation enters into force | 
| Initial battery requirements | At least three main components, including the cells, must be EU-made | 
| Stricter battery requirements | Minimum number of EU-made components rises to five three years after the legislation enters into force Cells, cathode active materials and battery management systems (BMS) must be EU-made | 
| Drivetrains and electronic systems | Electric drivetrains and main electronic systems must each achieve an EU-made share of at least 50% three years after the legislation enters into force Share calculated using component ex-works prices | 
| Small EV derogation | M1E vehicles assembled within the EU must satisfy either of the following: ① An EU-made share of at least 70% for vehicle components excluding the battery ② At least three EU-made main battery components, including the cells | 
UK Auto Industry Faces Twin Burdens of Rules of Origin and Tariffs
The EU’s preference for domestic production has complicated the calculations facing the UK, which has maintained supply-chain links with the bloc since Brexit. Separately from the IAA, battery rules of origin under the EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement are scheduled to tighten next year. The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) estimates that 82% of the 520,000 electric passenger cars and vans due to be exported from the EU to the UK next year will fail to meet those rules and incur a 10% tariff. UK automakers have consequently requested a phased deferral of local sourcing obligations for battery cells and cathode materials. These pressures could strengthen the UK’s incentive to rebuild closer economic ties with the EU. British industry is already seeking assurances that domestic companies will not be disadvantaged by the EU’s “Made in Europe” policies, while the two sides continue discussions on the scope of UK participation.
As part of this process, the UK is also considering additional tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles. The EU reportedly called for higher tariffs on Chinese vehicles and closer trade-policy coordination during discussions over UK participation in the IAA. Options under consideration within the British government include raising tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles to EU levels. No final decision has been made, however, amid concerns that Chinese retaliation could harm exports to China by British automakers, including Jaguar Land Rover. The UK government is continuing consultations with industry, saying its response will reflect the interests of domestic industry and the wider economy.
Korean Companies Targeting Europe Shift Component Sourcing Locally
South Korea faces similarly complex calculations. A strategy combining increased European production with greater local component sourcing is expected to become more important for Korean manufacturers. Components meeting EU origin requirements could be better placed to secure demand from automakers that need to increase their domestic sourcing shares. Korean component suppliers serving Hyundai and Kia’s European factories could also use their local manufacturing bases to expand business with European automakers. Converting that demand into orders, however, will require both additional production capacity and a review of sourcing arrangements for key materials and components. With batteries and electric drivetrains subject to separate localization standards, companies need to assess the requirements for EU-origin status item by item. Given the time needed to expand local facilities, investment and procurement plans must align regulatory implementation dates with customers’ schedules for bringing new models into series production.
Korean component manufacturers are already expanding their European production footprints. Automotive component specialist Hyundai Wia began series production on September 30 at its new factory in Martin, Slovakia, following an investment of approximately $29.9 million. After establishing a local subsidiary in April 2023, the company had been manufacturing constant-velocity joints at an existing facility before relocating production to the new plant to accommodate anticipated volume growth. The new factory has annual capacity for constant-velocity joints, which transmit power to the wheels, for 800,000 vehicles, and coolant modules for 280,000 vehicles. Drivetrain and thermal-management components produced there are intended for models including the Kia EV2 and EV4. Hyundai Wia plans further investment to increase constant-velocity joint capacity by as much as fivefold and expand production to heating, ventilation and air-conditioning modules. In line with those plans, it intends to increase local employment from 98 workers currently to approximately 410 by 2030.
Chinese Automakers Face Pressures on Both Exports and European Production
Chinese automakers face the most pressing need to respond to Europe’s tighter regulations. With weak domestic demand, overcapacity and price competition squeezing profitability, Europe is regarded as a pivotal market for securing sales volumes and earnings. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), Europe accounted for approximately 40% of the value of Chinese-made electric vehicle exports in 2024. Vehicles manufactured in China can command higher prices in Europe than at home, making the region important for Chinese companies seeking to bolster profitability through overseas operations. Chery has likewise presented overseas sales as a means of enhancing brand value and profitability. With additional tariffs already imposed on this market and domestic production and sourcing requirements now being pursued, Chinese manufacturers face rising export costs alongside heavier local investment burdens.

Eroding trust and respect undermines Seoul-Washington alliance
Under President Donald Trump's administration, stricter immigration policies have led to an increase in the U.S. rejecting visa applications for visitors from around the globe. It is one thing for a government to reject potentially dangerous travelers, but it is another matter when the applicants are lawmakers from allied countries whose travel is halted by a visa denial.
Rep. Jin Sung-joon of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) and chairman of South Korea's National Assembly Defense Committee saw his visa application, submitted on Oct. 12, rejected. He planned to visit the U.S. Indo-Pacific Command in Hawaii from Sunday to Thursday with a delegation of members from the defense committee.
"It disregards the standing of Korea’s National Assembly and undermines the mutual respect and trust that form the foundation of the U.S.-Korea alliance," Jin wrote in a Facebook post after the rejection.
Former DPK chairman Rep. Jung Chung-rae also had his U.S. visa application stalled, disabling his planned visit to the United States for a parliamentary audit of Seoul's diplomatic mission.
Refusals of visas — in this case A-2 official visas for ranking ruling party lawmakers — are not a common occurrence. The denials are especially unusual given the long path the United States and Korea have walked together as allies. Repeated refusals have prompted speculation in Seoul that Washington may be using the visa denials to signal its discontent.
Sticking points in several issues, including the transfer of wartime operational control from Washington to Seoul and the role of U.S. forces in South Korea have created the appearance of a rift that Seoul has sought to characterize as part of a “normal” relationship between the two countries.
There are also perceived differences over trade issues, including the U.S. company Coupang and concerns in Washington that the Lee Jae Myung administration is taking a more progressive approach, particularly in its relations with China. These points of friction persist even as Lee reiterates a pragmatic approach to diplomacy and a strong emphasis on the Korea-U.S. alliance.
The refusal of B-1 and B2 visitor visas for Koreans also increased in 2025. Based on data from the foreign ministry submitted to Rep. Kim Dae-sik of the People Power Party, a total of 24.73 percent of Korean U.S. visa applicants had their applications rejected, a rise of 9.76 percent over 2024 numbers. That means 1 out of 4 Koreans applying for a U.S. visa last year had it denied.
The A-2 visas sought by Jin and Jung are intended for official visits, although applications are still subject to consular screening. Both were student activists in the 1980s and 1990s, but neither had encountered difficulties during previous official visits to the United States.
Even taking into account the rigorous screening system, it is not an ordinary turn of events to see parliamentarians have their U.S. visa applications turned down. Any differences between the two allies should be addressed through direct, face-to-face consultations rather than by preventing such meetings from taking place. For Korea, one of Washington’s few treaty allies on the Asian continent, the denials are an extraordinary development that risks unnecessarily inflaming tensions and perceptions of a widening rift.
The two countries’ ambassadors have also acknowledged challenges in the relationship. Korean Ambassador to the U.S. Kang Kyung-wha told a recent parliamentary audit that she faced “limitations” in communicating with the White House. The embassy later clarified that her remarks reflected a desire for more frequent communication with U.S. officials. Meanwhile, U.S. Ambassador to Korea Michelle Steel recently described bilateral relations as being in “turbulence.”
As the geopolitical and geosecurity landscape shifts amid heightened global uncertainty, alliances may invariably be put to the test. Still, Korea is a longtime alliance partner of the U.S. It remains a dedicated security and economic partner. Both sides should therefore avoid actions that could be perceived as deliberate slights or attempts to pressure one another over differences. Mutual respect and trust are essential to strengthening the alliance.
